title: The Note You Come Back To
summary: Some notes only make sense months later. Why hindsight rewrites your memory, how to write a note your future self can use, and what to do when you read it again.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
You're cleaning out an old notes file and find a line from March, squeezed between a meeting reminder and half a release checklist: "Retry logic in sync feels off. Too many places decide when to retry." No ticket, no follow-up. Back then it was just a hunch.

It's November now. Last month, an incident report traced a duplicate-message bug to two layers retrying the same request. Read today, that March line is suddenly a lot more interesting. You noticed something eight months before you could explain it.

Some notes pay off right away: a command, a decision, the steps to reproduce a bug. Others are slower. They aren't ready to be a design doc or a lesson yet. They're markers you left when something caught your attention and you didn't know what to do with it. Those notes only show their value on the second read. This post is about that second read: why it's worth doing, and how to write notes that survive it.

Your memory edits the past. Your notes don't.

Psychologist Baruch Fischhoff tested this in a classic set of three experiments (Hindsight ≠ foresight: the effect of outcome knowledge on judgment under uncertainty). People who were told how a situation turned out rated that outcome as more likely than people who weren't told. They also overestimated what they would have known without the outcome, and they were "largely unaware" that knowing the ending had changed their judgment.

That's hindsight bias, and it's why "I knew it all along" is so unreliable. Once you know how the retry bug ended, your memory rewrites what you thought in March, without asking you. Maybe you'll remember being more certain than you were. Maybe you'll forget you noticed anything at all.

A dated note is the one witness that can't be edited. It shows what you actually saw, with what you knew at the time. Sometimes that's good news: you spotted something early, and you can trust that instinct a bit more next time. Sometimes it's a correction: the thing you were sure about in March turned out to be wrong, and now you can see exactly where your reasoning slipped.

Most notes are a bucket

Andy Matuschak, who has written a lot about how people think with notes, puts it bluntly: most people use notes as a bucket for storage or scratch thoughts, and "most 'storage-oriented' notes will never be useful again" (his note on the subject). The kind he cares about are what he calls evergreen notes, notes "written and organized to evolve, contribute, and accumulate over time, across projects."

You don't need a whole system to get some of that benefit. You just need to come back. A scrap you never reread stays a scrap. One you reread, question and update starts to build on itself.

Write it so future you can use it

A note that says "sync weird??" is useless in eight months. A few extra seconds when you write it make the return worth it:

  • A date. Without one, you can't tell what you knew then.
  • One line of context: which PR, which meeting, which incident made you stop.
  • What you think, plus what would prove you wrong. "I think the retries will collide under load. I'd be wrong if the queue already dedupes by message ID."
  • A word or tag you'll actually search for later.

That third line does the most work. Once you write down what would prove you wrong, the vague feeling becomes a small bet, and a bet is something you can check.

What to do on the second read

Pick a regular slot, like twenty minutes on the last Friday of the month, and read back through what you wrote. For each note that still pulls at you, ask:

  • Is this still true? Did the months since then confirm it, complicate it or prove it wrong?
  • What do I know now that I didn't when I wrote it?
  • Who else should see this?

Then do one of three things. Delete it, because plenty of notes were only useful in the moment. Leave it as raw material. Or promote it: rewrite it as a clearer paragraph, a checklist item, a decision record, a ticket, a message to the teammate who owns that code.

You'll also notice something nice along the way. The problems you once described in confused half-sentences now have names. Decisions that felt scary are routine. Progress is hard to see while you're in it, and an old page is one of the few places you can see how far you've come.

If the hard part for you is writing the note in the first place, this post on the first rough note is for you. If you want to build the daily habit, try what thirty days of small notes can teach.

Try this week

  • Open a notes file from three or more months ago and read it for ten minutes.
  • Pick one note and mark it: confirmed, complicated or wrong.
  • Next time you write a hunch down, add the date and one line on what would prove you wrong.
  • Put a 20-minute "reread notes" slot on your calendar for the end of the month.

faqs.q: Why should I reread old notes?
faqs.a: Because your memory isn't a reliable record of what you thought. Hindsight bias research by Baruch Fischhoff found that once people know an outcome, they overestimate what they would have known without it. A dated note shows what you actually noticed at the time.

faqs.q: What makes a note useful months later?
faqs.a: A date, one line of context (which PR, meeting or incident), what you think plus what would prove you wrong, and a word you'll search for later. Without the date and context, an old note is hard to judge.

faqs.q: What should I do with old notes when I review them?
faqs.a: Ask whether each note was confirmed, complicated or proved wrong, then delete it, keep it as raw material or promote it into something clearer: a checklist item, a decision record, a ticket or a message to the right teammate.
